body.objective: Students will be able to identify production roles.
successCriteria: I can describe the main production roles
I can explain what cues are and how they are called
I can operate basic lighting or sound safely
body.hook: For every actor you see on stage, there may be ten people you never see: designers, builders, operators and the stage manager calling every cue. A show can survive a forgotten line. It can't survive a missed blackout or a set that falls over.

vocabulary.definition: The person who runs rehearsals and calls all cues during performances.
A signal for a lighting, sound or scene change.
The person who designs how the stage is lit.
The person who plans music and sound effects.
People who move sets and props and run the show backstage.
A rehearsal focused on running lights, sound and scene changes.
The stage manager's script with all blocking and cues.

study.title: Behind the Scenes
study.question: What do technical theatre roles do, and how do they work together?
study.passage:
Production roles: Director (overall vision), stage manager (runs rehearsals, keeps the prompt book, calls cues), lighting designer and operator, sound designer and operator, set designer and builders, costume designer, props master, house manager (audience and front of house).
Part 1, Role jigsaw (10 minutes): Each group researches one role and teaches the class: main job, key skills, when they work (rehearsal or performance).
Part 2, Cue sheet (15 minutes): Read a short scene and write a cue sheet. Each cue has a number, a trigger (a line or action), and what happens. Example: LX 1 (lighting), trigger "Lights up," state: warm general wash. SQ 1 (sound), trigger "She opens the window," effect: birdsong.
Part 3, Calling cues (15 minutes): The stage manager says "Stand by LX 2," the operator answers "Standing by," then "LX 2, go." Practise with the lighting board or a simple app and a speaker.
Safety: never look directly into lights, never touch hot lamps, keep cables taped down, wear closed-toe shoes backstage.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; roles and cueing conventions from standard theatre practice.

study.product: Run the cues for a classmate's scene: write a cue sheet with at least four lighting and three sound cues, then call or operate them in a performance.

practice.q: What does a stage manager do?

practice.a: A signal for a lighting, sound or scene change.
Moves sets and props and runs backstage.
A rehearsal focused on lights, sound and scene changes.
The stage manager's script with blocking and cues.

practice.q: What do LX and SQ stand for in a cue sheet?
What are the three parts of a cue?
What is the reply to "Stand by sound 2"?
What does the house manager do?
practice.a: Looks after the audience and front of house.
Tape cables, don't touch hot lights, wear closed-toe shoes.

practice.q: What does a lighting designer decide?
practice.a: How the stage is lit, including colour, angle and intensity.
So everyone knows exactly which cue is next.
Colour, brightness and angle make scenes feel warm, cold, tense or calm.

practice.q: Why does a technical rehearsal sometimes take hours?
practice.a: Every cue must be set, timed and tested.

practice.q: How do designers support the director's vision?
practice.a: They create lighting, sound, sets and costumes that match the director's concept.

misconceptions: Thinking the director runs the show during performances
Thinking technical theatre is less important than acting
Thinking operators should take cues on their own timing
exitTicket: Name three production roles and what they do.
Write one lighting cue with a number, trigger and effect.

items.q: Who calls cues during a performance?
items.answer: D) the stage manager

items.q: A cue is
options: B) a line of dialogue only
D) a signal for a technical change
items.answer: D) a signal for a technical change

items.q: The crew
options: A) moves sets and props backstage
items.answer: A) moves sets and props backstage

items.q: A technical rehearsal focuses on
options: B) lights, sound and scene changes
items.answer: B) lights, sound and scene changes

items.q: In a cue sheet, SQ means
items.answer: A) sound cue

items.q: The reply to "Stand by LX 5" is
items.answer: A) "Standing by."

items.q: A cue's trigger is
options: A) the line or action that signals it
items.answer: A) the line or action that signals it

items.q: The house manager is responsible for
options: A) the audience and front of house
items.answer: A) the audience and front of house

items.q: The prompt book contains
options: B) the script with blocking and cues
items.answer: B) the script with blocking and cues

items.q: Why does one person call all cues?
options: A) To keep timing coordinated and consistent
items.answer: A) To keep timing coordinated and consistent

items.q: A loose cable across a walkway should be
items.answer: B) taped down or rerouted

items.q: A lighting designer can create tension by
options: B) using harsh angles, shadows or cold colours
items.answer: B) using harsh angles, shadows or cold colours

items.q: What does a stage manager do?
items.answer: Runs rehearsals and calls all cues in performance.

items.q: Define cue.
items.answer: A signal for a lighting, sound or scene change.

items.q: Write a sound cue for thunder when a character says "Here comes the storm."
items.answer: SQ number, trigger line, effect thunder.

items.q: Explain the standby and go system.
items.answer: The stage manager warns "Stand by," the operator replies, then the SM says "Go" at the trigger.

items.q: Name two backstage safety rules.
items.answer: Tape cables, don't touch hot lights, closed-toe shoes, never look into lights.

items.q: Describe the job of a sound designer.
items.answer: Plans music and sound effects that support the play.

items.q: Explain how technical roles support the story.
items.answer: Lights, sound, sets and costumes create mood, time, place and focus.

items.q: Describe what could go wrong without a technical rehearsal.
items.answer: Missed or mistimed cues, unsafe scene changes, wrong levels.
